newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq gets oil flowing, proclaims victory over U.S..
newsitem.headline: Iraq gets oil flowing, proclaims victory over U.S..

text.p: Iraq got its oil flowing to the outside world on Wednesday and state-run newspapers hailed the resumption of exports after a six-year break as a victory over U.S. policies towards Baghdad.
"The will of the steadfast and patient Iraq triumphed and all U.S. obstacles have gone in vain," said the ruling Baath party newspaper al-Thawra in a front-page editorial.
Other newspapers said the flow of Iraqi crude marked the start of the process to dismantle all sanctions against Iraq.
"The embargo has cracked," said the government newspaper al-Jumhouriya in a banner headline.

President Saddam Hussein pressed the button to start Iraqi oil flowing through a pipeline to Turkey on Tuesday for the first time since 1990, when U.N. sanctions were imposed after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait.

Iraq was allowed to resume limited exports of oil worth $2 billion every six months under a closely monitored oil-for-food deal with the United Nations intended to alleviate the suffering of ordinary Iraqis.
The official Iraqi News Agency (INA) said the trade ministry started signing food deals with foreign firms on Wednesday.

INA, quoting trade minister Mohammed Mehdi Saleh, said each Iraqi would be entitled, once food reaches Iraq, to a monthly ration of nine kg of flour instead of seven, and 2.5 kg of rice instead of the current 1.25.
The sugar ration would go up to two kg from 750 grams. Baby formula, tea and soap rations also go up.
On Monday night Iraqis celebrated the imminent return of their oil to world markets by firing guns and singing and dancing in Baghdad.

There were conflicting reports on whether oil actually reached Turkey's Ceyhan terminal on Tuesday. But on Wednesday Turkey's state-run Anatolian news agency said oil was reaching Ceyhan at an expected rate of 350,000 barrels per day.
Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad denied reports that Iraqi oil had been disrupted on Tuesday because of problems, "whether political or technical", INA reported.

Taha Hamud Mosa, senior undersecretary of Iraq's oil ministry, told Reuters a small technical problem had held up the flow of Iraqi crude to Turkey for a short time but Iraqi technicians solved it very quickly.
"There was a small fault. We have overcome that very quickly. Oil is now ready to flow any time," he said.
He said Iraq had cleared a deal with Turkish refiners Tupras for the loading of 75,000 barrels per day of oil and the Turkish company would lift the crude within 24 hours.
"There is no problem at the moment," said Mosa. "Part of the problem raised earlier was because we did not have ready deals."

An official of SOMO, the state organisation for marketing oil, said foreign companies were "coming in droves" to Baghdad for oil deals. He said demand for Iraqi oil was higher than the limit of about 650,000 barrels a day set by the United Nations.

Economic sanctions on Iraq remain in place until Iraq complies with Gulf War resolutions, among them the dismantling of its weapons of mass destruction -- the task of chief U.N. weapons inspector Rolf Ekeus who is currently visiting Iraq.

Ekeus said Iraq and the United Nations had agreed to put off a dispute over removing scrapped missile engines until February next year. Iraq last month prevented U.N. arms inspectors from moving the engines outside the country for analysis, an issue that Ekeus described as a serious breach of a U.N. Security Council resolution.
Asked how many more banned missiles the United Nations thought lraq was still hiding, he told reporters: "It is a significant number that is not accounted for."
